entry.dc:title: Shallow coal: a hidden resource for urban regeneration
entry.dc:creator: Grimshaw P.
entry.dc:description: An ironic legacy of the Industrial Revolution is the large amounts of shallow coal buried under its factories and houses. As these areas become ripe for redevelopment there is an opportunity to reclaim the land by the process of opencast mining. The article describes five areas: Bilston, in the West Midlands; Wednesbury, Rotherham and Tinsley Park in Yorkshire; and Merthy Tydfil in Wales where over 10 million tonnes of coal have been mined and 653ha of land reclaimed for after-use as shops, airports, housing or industry. -A.Gilg

entry.dc:title: Deforestation and soil degradation in Sierra Leone: the role of forest removal and upland erosion in a rural catchment under multiple uses
entry.dc:creator: Bomah A.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Ecology Environmental Sciences
entry.dc:description: In Sierra Leone, the most important human activities in rural areas include shifting cultivation, brush firing, opencast mining, commercial forest harvesting of firewood and timber and suburban development. The inherent characteristics of land attributes which are more visible expressions of land degradation were measured in a typical catchment in the eastern part of the country to explain the variation of soil erosion taking place. Human activities in the catchment are leading to degradation the most important of which is soil erosion. All the land attributes studied operate simultaneously in the degradation processes. This is because the farmers indiscriminately clear and cultivate these lands paying no attention to the land attributes and management strategies. This is a result dampens the predominant role of any one attribute in land degradation. -from Authors

entry.dc:title: Technology upgradation, new technology and R&D in Coal India
entry.dc:creator: Narayanan M.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: For the next several years, coal India's proposed strategy is development and adoption of new technologies, and commercialisation of technologies established with R&D work. The major areas where work on the strategy has been taken up are coal exploration, shaft sinking, mine development, mine construction, underground mining, opencast mining, coal handling, coal beneficiation, coal combustion, slurry pipeline transport, environmental management, and The areas for further R&D work are an in-seam seismic survey, detection of sub-surface cavities in abandoned underground workings, evaluation of hydrogeological parameters by geophysical methods, and stochastic modelling of the structures of the coal fields for assessing exploration work.

entry.dc:title: Environmental aspects of opencast mining with reference to the Rother Valley Country Park
entry.dc:creator: Brook C.
entry.dc:description: The environmental aspects which affect open-cast coalmining are broadly those which arise during the period of working the site and those relating to the restoration and after use of the land. The paper considers both these aspects and relates to the working of the Meadowgate opencast coal site and its restoration as the Rother Valley Country Park. This country park provides a wide range of outdoor leisure activities, at the same time incorporating extensive flood protection works, and demonstrates how an opencast restoration can be designed to improve the environment and maximise the benefit to the public.

entry.dc:title: The Lausitz "bottle' clay - a ceramic accompanying raw material of brown coal open cast mining in the past and future
entry.dc:creator: Lincke L.
entry.dc:description: The Lausitz "bottle'-clay is the raw material base to produce bricks. At the end of our millennium the today used "bottle'-clay deposits will be mined or will be overdredged in connection with coal mining. So, the mining of "bottle'-clay in connection with brown-coal mining is necessary to maintain the brick production after the year 2000. Today that would be already possible in the "bottle'-clay deposits in the east field of the brown-coal opencast mining Nochten. Extensive prospection and projection work is necessary to prepare that combined mining. -English summary

entry.dc:title: Use of quantitative complex interpretation of bore-hole measurements for tips of opencast mining
entry.dc:creator: Zwingmann A.
entry.dc:description: The possibilities of geophysical bore-hole measurements and the direct deduction of soil-physical data to investigate tips are discussed at one example. An estimation of results allows to suppose possible use of them with higher exactness. -English summary

entry.dc:title: Changes in the microbial community and physico‐chemical characteristics of topsoils stockpiled during opencast mining
entry.dc:creator: Harris J.
entry.dc:description: Abstract. Experiments on the effects of stockpiling soil on an opencast coal mine in Derbyshire showed that there were significant changes in the microbial community. Numbers of aerobic bacteria in stored soils ranged from 0.5 to 12.8 ± 10<sup>7</sup> colony‐forming‐units (CFU)g<sup>‐1</sup> with the smallest values being in the deepest parts of the oldest stores, whereas an adjacent undisturbed soil contained 6.6 ± 10<sup>7</sup> CFU g<sup>‐1</sup>. There was a greater effect on the numbers of fungal spores, which ranged from 0.1 to 6.7 ± 10<sup>5</sup> CFU g<sup>‐1</sup> soil, all less than the 10 ± 10<sup>5</sup> CFU g<sup>‐1</sup> recorded for the undisturbed control soil. The number of fungal spores in the deepest part of the older soil stores was only 1/100 of the number in the undisturbed soil. This was mirrored by the biomass values, as determined by adenosine triphosphate (ATP) assay. Values of ATP ranged from 0.38 to 13.13 nmol g<sup>‐1</sup> as compared to 5.8 nmol g<sup>‐1</sup> in the undisturbed soil. All three of these microbiological properties decreased in value with both age and depth of storage. Neither anaerobic nor spore‐forming bacterial numbers were greatly affected by storage. The pH values tended toward neutrality in the deeper parts of the soil stores, and there was less organic matter in the older stores. Copyright © 1989, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

entry.dc:title: Environmental assessment for opencast coal mining
entry.dc:creator: Coppin N.
entry.dc:description: Provides a discussion of the background to an examination of the assessment of environmental impacts both in the short and the long term. It describes the procedural aspects of environmental assessments for opencast mining and details technical aspects before considering the benefits to be achieved. -from Land & Minerals Surveying

entry.dc:title: A review of the bureaucratic, political and legislative problems encountered in the reclamation of the plateau tinfields of Nigeria
entry.dc:creator: Alexander M.J.
entry.dc:description: In most countries today, consent given by government for opencast mining activities usually includes strict regulations governing the restoration and reclamation of the area once mining operations have ceased. Even in the developed countries of Europe and North America, such legislation is frequently of relatively recent origin and requires strong political willingness for enforcement. In countries such as those in Africa, where mineral resources were often first exploited by the colonial powers, the introduction and enforcement of reclamation legislation has proved extremely difficult. This paper examines the problems the authorities on the Jos Plateau of Nigeria have encountered in attempting to implement the reclamation clauses of the Minerals Act introduced in 1946 in the laws of Nigeria. Commercial opencast tin mining was begun on the Jos Plateau by the Niger Company in 1904. From the outset, whilst all mining activities were controlled by legislation governing granting of leases and compensation rates for loss of land, no requirement for the restoration of land after tin extraction was placed on the mining companies. Thus, with the introduction of non-retrospective legislation in the 1946 Minerals Act, only mining operations started after the date of enactment were covered by the restoration and reclamation clauses. Unfortunately, neither the legislation requiring restoration nor the operation of the Reclamation Unit established to deal with reclamation of sites worked before 1946, can be considered to be a success. The reasons for the almost complete failure of this legislation is examined in some detail, and it is argued that the lack of success of the policies is attributable primarily to political rivalries both within the State legislatures and between the State and Federal Governments. In recent years economic problems have added to the difficulties facing those involved in attempting to reclaim the "devastated" areas of the Plateau. With the temporary, economically-enforced lull in reclamation activities, it is suggested that a major reappraisal of reclamation strategy is required in order to ensure that maximum benefit is obtained from the derelict mined areas. © 1989.

entry.dc:title: Shear strength characteristics of sandstones of an opencast mining block, Jharia coalfield, India
entry.dc:creator: Gupta K.K.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: Application of a non-linear failure criterion and non-linear regression analysis (NLRA) determine the material constants and other curve defining constants which give shear strength characteristics more precisely. A Fortran computer program I3XIER was developed for carrying out NLRA. The program J3XIER was developed for highly jointed/broken rock. Triaxial data of eleven tests conducted on sand-stones occuring in a rockmass in an opencast mining block in Jharia Coalfield were analysed by I3XIER. A sample input/output and a sample plot are presented. Shear strength characteristics of the rockmass were required for conducting slope stability analysis. A 140 m section of the strata will be affected when the open pit will reach a depth of about 120 m.

entry.dc:title: Opencast mining noise
entry.dc:creator: Walker A.
entry.dc:description: Coal occurs in seams of varying thickness overlain and interleaved by layers of soil and other materials, loosely described as overburden. It is largely the removal, storage and replacement of the overburden which gives rise to most of the environmental consequences of opencast coaling, including noise. In this feature three aspects of the issue of environmental noise are considered: Sources of Noise; Noise Criteria; and the Control of Noise.

entry.dc:title: Ballymoney lignite project. Hydrology and environmental assessment
entry.dc:creator: Finlayson D.
entry.dc:description: This article discusses the role of hydrology in environmental assessment, against the background of studies carried out into the feasibility of opencast mining of lignite at Ballymoney in Northern Ireland. These studies were carried out for Mekatharra (NI) Ltd, a subsidiary of Meekatharra Minerals of Syndey Australia, during 1987 and 1988. The work was to establish the base feasibility, costs and output characteristics of the development as a possible source of fuel for a 450MW minemouth power station, as a potential element in the development of generating capacity in Northern Ireland. Other alternatives then being considered by the Department of Economic Development (DED) in Northern Ireland included a lignite mine at Crumlin, being supported by BP Coal Ltd, and further development at Kilroot power station on the East Antrim coast. Hydrotechnica Ltd were also responsible for hyrological studies of the Crumlin project.

entry.dc:title: Mining technology - an overview
entry.dc:creator: Banerjee A.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of the Institution of Engineers India Mining Engineering Division
entry.dc:description: According to the author, the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act should be suitably amended to provide a corporate incentive to the mining industry to plan the mines with a view to bring about a change in the environment management concepts with particular reference to reclamation of mined land. Unless this is done, no amount of legislative measure alone will be able to place the large scale opencast mining in coal, lignite and other minerals, in a position to make a meaningful contribution to the economy despite introduction of the latest hardware. The present trend if carried forward to the 21st century, which starts only 12 years from now, will retard economic growth.

entry.dc:title: New crusher system for working with mobile plants
entry.dc:creator: Snell D.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: A new type of crushing machine, a continuous crusher, has found application to opencast working in recent times. The crushing machine is a combination of a crusher and a feeder and has the possibility of working a complete crushing plant at ground level. According to design, the horizontal crusher can be loaded horizontally by loading shovels or it can be equipped with a loading bunker lying at the most 3 m above ground and which can be reached without a ramp. There are currently about 30 plants of this type in operation. Of these, one third stands in quarries, a third is used in large coal and oil shale opencast mining fields and a third is working in recycling building materials from building and industrial demolitions.

entry.dc:title: Application of deep diaphrach walls for groundwater control in opencast lignite nining in the German Democratic Republic
entry.dc:creator: Mielcarek W.
entry.dc:description: In the German Democratic Republic, about 95% of highly saturated lignite deposits, mined by opencast mining methods, are drained by dewatering wells. However, in order to reduce the surface water inflow to an excavation through sub-soil and to minimize the number of dewatering wells and to effect financial and material savings deep impermeable diapaphragm walls are being increasingly used. In order to meet the requirements of modern opencast mining technology, these diaphragm walls are some 100m deep and extend for a continuous length of several kilometers. Consequently, the well known technique of constructing diaphram walls by the discontinuous pile and section method has been replaced by the newly developed continuous leading pile method. As a result of research and development, this new method of excavating deep trenches utilises a horizontally rotating twin screw shaft device. This technique can excavate a trench in soil from the surface to its final depth by continuously advancing in a lateral direction. Two further technical modifications to this device have been carried out to improve its operational efficiency. The paper describes the application of deep diaphragm walls in the control of groundwater in opencast lignite mining. © 1988 Springer-Verlag.

entry.dc:title: REVIEW OF BLAST DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS IN QUARRYING AND OPENCAST MINING PART 2 INITIATION AND COMPUTERIZED DESIGN.
entry.dc:creator: Ball M.
entry.dc:description: With the development of modern drilling equipment capable of drilling blast-holes cleanly and accurately and advanced surveying equipment for the precise determination of quarry face profiles, blasting design is simpler and more predictable. The use of computers may also predict blast results and permits adjustments to blast patterns and choice of explosives without recourse to implementing these in the field. In spite of these modern aids to blast design, safe blasts need not necessarily follow accurate measurement and computer-aided design. It is a combination of these factors with understanding on the part of the operator which will ultimately lead to safe and efficient blasts. The computer aided design method SABREX is described.

entry.dc:title: Opencast mining in Great Britain
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Since the beginning of the 1980s British Coal's opencast coal production in Great Britain has been maintained at about 14Mt/y, a rate of output which has met the requirements of the market without causing undue disturbance to the environment. Opencast coal recovery methods allow seams of only 100mm-150mm to be worked profitably in association with thicker coal seams. However, difficulties in finding sites, the role of opencast in balancing the quality of deep-mined coal, and public hostility all combine to make opencast mining an activity beset with controversy. Colliery Guardian's review of opencast mining is based on the revised edition of the Opencast Executive's explanatory brochure. Production costs are given.

entry.dc:title: Recent developments in explosives techniques: Testing and safety aspects of non-permitted explosives
entry.dc:creator: Bhattacharyya M.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: With growing emphasis on large-scale opencast mining, the need for efficient and, as far as possible, hazard free explosives has become inevitable. The explosives industry in India, since its beginning in 1958, has been developing continually to keep pace with this growing need of the country, and with the infrastructural facilities, CMRS have always encouraged the indigenous development of explosives. As a result of all these efforts, India is now self sufficient in meeting its requirement of explosives. Explosives showing satisfactory performance under the regular tests and not required to be put through the safety tests in respect of their incendivity are designated as non-permitted explosives. Such explosives are suitable for use in opencast mining of coal, rock and other minerals and in underground metaliferrous mine workings.

entry.dc:title: A REVIEW OF BLAST DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS IN QUARRYING AND OPENCAST MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Ball M.
entry.dc:description: Good blasts are the result of the correct choice of explosives, and good blast design. The diameter, length and inclination of blast holes, drilling pattern, type, quantity and utilization of explosives, rock type, firing sequence and delay timing all have an effect on the efficiency of the overall operation. If the highest overall efficiency and highest safety standards are to be achieved, all blasts must be properly designed and recorded for future reference. This paper reviews the basic factors leading to good design and discusses the role of computer-aided design and in particular the SABREX computer blast model.

entry.dc:title: NALCO - an epoch in mine development
entry.dc:creator: Mohanty D.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: The discovery of over 1000 million tonnes of bauxite deposits on the east coast of India in the mid seventies has placed the country in the forefront on the world bauxite map. National Aluminum Company Limited (NALCO) was formed to exploit and utilize the rich bauxite resources with the following units: a bauxite mine to raise 2.4 million tonnes per year of bauxite; an alumina plant to produce 800,000 tonnes per year of coarse alumina; an aluminum plant of 218,000 tonnes capacity per year; a captive power plant with an installed capacity of 600 MW; and port facilities. The state-of-art technology, meticulous planning, efficient project management, prudent manpower selection and careful training at NALCO mines have given us a quantum jump and now, the Indian mining industry can take-off to be a forerunner in the field of opencast mining.

entry.dc:title: Opencast mining machinery and productivity at Neyveli Lignite Mines
entry.dc:creator: Sundaramurthy T.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of the Institution of Engineers India Mining Engineering Division
entry.dc:description: The problems associated with mining lignite at Neyveli, India, the mining and auxiliary equipment used and the special modifications incorporated in them, the transportation facilities, the method used to dispose off the overburden and achievements of the organization, are discussed. Lignite mining conditions are examined. The continuous method of mining is discussed as are capacity and size changes in mining equipment.

entry.dc:title: TECHNOLOGICAL UPGRADATION AND MODERNISATION OF METALLIFEROUS MINES IN INDIA.
entry.dc:creator: Choudhuri S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: The emergence of the public sector as the prominent leader in the core sector and demand for bulk production and productivity improvements has brought about major changes in the technological profile of mining industry especially after the sixties. The first technological upgradation and modernization was adopted by the iron ore mines of NMDC and Hindusthan Steel Ltd. (presently SAIL) for opencast mining and by Hindusthan Copper Ltd. in respect of underground mining for the Khetri copper complex. Other mining enterprises have followed suit. The author reviews these developments.

entry.dc:title: LATEST TECHNIQUES IN COAL AND ROCK DRILLING.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: The proving of coal reserves, the extraction of overburden in opencast mining, the drivage of underground gate-roads and the fixing of roof bolts for support depend, to a large extent, on the use of rock drills and associated equipment. The drilling equipment chosen by any drilling contractor is based upon the contractor's experience and the economic environment in which it is operating. It is utilized to achieve the most cost effective means of drilling a borehole, while maintaining the quality of the end product, i. e. , the borehole and the geological information obtained from it.

entry.dc:title: Some physical features of soil after opencast mining
entry.dc:creator: King J.A.
entry.dc:description: Abstract. The soil of a restored opencast site in Northumberland is described and compared with the surrounding undisturbed soil. The most serious change in the soil was increased bulk density at the surface of the subsoil (0.3 m depth). Only a small overall reduction in pore space occurred, at the expense of continuous macropores. More of the pore space in the restored soil occurred as fine fissures as opposed to biotic channels, and the restored soil was weaker because of subsoiling and a loss of stability in microstructures. These changes are discussed in relation to root exploration, water movement and land management. Copyright © 1988, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved
